reason: the question is what this port does with the key, and the answer follows from the three calls beside it: a key of the release's own keychain is signed and verified by the release's own SecKeyRawSign and SecKeyRawVerify, and no key at all can exchange, because the release has no elliptic key agreement and this package has no key of its own kind yet
effect: true for sign and verify with kSecKeyAlgorithmECDSASignatureDigestX962SHA256 or ...MessageX962SHA256, and false for everything else: for a key exchange (the release exports no elliptic key agreement, and the keys this package would make itself, which are the only ones the curve would serve, do not exist yet - SecKeyCreateWithData is still absent), for encrypt and decrypt, and for every other algorithm. A key carrying the port's own marker says true for a key exchange as well, beside the false the release's own key answers, and the same suite checks both: measured on the host.

reason: iOS 6.1.3 signs with a key of its own keychain through SecKeyRawSign, which it exports, so for such a key no curve is needed here; the curve is reached only for a key this package created and holds the scalar of, and no such key exists yet
effect: a DER ECDSA signature of the SHA-256 of the data, in the low-s half Apple's own SecKeyCreateSignature produces: kSecKeyRawSign is called with kSecPaddingNone, and with kSecPaddingPKCS1 once if the release refuses that, and the answer it gives is read as it is - the two 32 byte halves of a P-256 signature, or their DER, and a result that is neither is refused with errSecInternalError rather than guessed at. A nil key or data, an algorithm outside the two ECDSA ones, a digest that is not 32 bytes under a Digest algorithm, and the release's own refusal (its OSStatus) each answer NULL with a CFError in NSOSStatusErrorDomain. A key that carries the port's own marker instead - kCharonSecKeyScalar, which SecKeyCreateWithData would set and which no port entry point sets yet - is signed by the curve rather than by the release, and that half is measured on the host: the DER charon@micro-ecc writes verifies under the host's own SecKeyVerifySignature in tests/backports/host/seckeycurve. No key of the release's keychain carries the marker, so on a device this second path is not reached yet, and which padding an EC key of the release takes is what the queued emulator probe settles.

effect: true when the signature is one of that key's, false when it is not - a signature that is not a signature is a false and not an error, as the host answers - and the verification itself is the release's own SecKeyRawVerify, with the two halves read back out of the DER when the caller passes a DER; a nil argument or an algorithm outside the two ECDSA ones answers false with a CFError in NSOSStatusErrorDomain. The same marker-carrying key is verified by the same curve, and a signature the host's own SecKeyCreateSignature makes verifies through that reader, measured in the same suite.
